cards.statement: Helm can install the same chart as separate releases using different release names.
cards.explanation: Installing a chart under a new release name creates a separate Helm release. The installations can use different configuration values.

cards.statement: `helm rollback` restores the target's earlier revision number as the current number.
cards.explanation: A Helm rollback creates a new revision containing the target revision's configuration. Its revision number increases instead of returning to the target number.
cards.misconception: Rolling back restores both an earlier configuration and its earlier revision number.

cards.statement: Helm gives `--set` values precedence over conflicting settings in `--values` files.
cards.explanation: Values supplied with --set override conflicting settings in --values files during the same install or upgrade.

cards.statement: Helm gives the first `--values` file priority when several files override the same value.
cards.explanation: When several --values files define the same setting, Helm takes the value from the rightmost file.
cards.misconception: The first values file establishes overrides that later files leave unchanged.

cards.statement: `helm upgrade --reset-values` clears the release's previously stored `--set` values.
cards.explanation: Helm stores --set overrides with a release. An upgrade using --reset-values discards those saved overrides and starts from the chart's defaults.

cards.statement: `helm uninstall` retains a release's history by default after deleting its resources.
cards.explanation: Helm uninstall deletes the release history by default. Adding --keep-history retains that record after the resources are removed.
cards.misconception: Uninstalling a release preserves its history automatically.

cards.statement: `helm template` renders chart manifests locally by default for review before release installation.
cards.explanation: Helm template displays rendered Kubernetes manifests for inspection. The command leaves installation to a separate step.

cards.statement: `helm search repo` can search Artifact Hub before its repositories are added locally.
cards.explanation: Helm search repo searches the chart repositories added to the local Helm client. It reads their locally cached indexes.
cards.misconception: The repo search command searches Artifact Hub independently of locally configured repositories.

cards.statement: `helm install` accepts a chart reference from an OCI registry as its installation source.
cards.explanation: Helm install accepts OCI chart references. This uses an OCI registry as the chart source instead of a traditional chart repository.

cards.statement: Helm 4's first upgrade of a Helm 3 release uses server-side apply by default.
cards.explanation: When Helm 4 first upgrades a Helm 3 release, it keeps client-side apply by default. An explicit --server-side override changes the method.
cards.misconception: Helm 4 applies its new-install default automatically to releases created with Helm 3.

cards.statement: `kubectl kustomize` can apply its rendered resources to the current cluster as part of the same command.
cards.explanation: kubectl kustomize prints the rendered resources. Use kubectl apply -k to apply the kustomization to the cluster.
cards.misconception: The rendering command also applies the resulting objects to the cluster.

source.title: Declarative Management of Kubernetes Objects Using Kustomize

cards.statement: Kustomize can render a base on its own when overlays add environment-specific patches to that base.
cards.explanation: A base references its own resources and has no knowledge of its overlays. Overlay patches affect the overlay's build, leaving a direct base build unchanged.

source.title: Declarative Management of Kubernetes Objects Using Kustomize

cards.statement: By default, Kustomize changes a generated ConfigMap's name when configMapGenerator content changes.
cards.explanation: Kustomize appends a content hash to generated ConfigMap names. Changed input produces a different suffix, and Kustomize updates references to the generated name.

source.title: Declarative Management of Kubernetes Objects Using Kustomize

cards.statement: Kustomize selects patch targets satisfying either the name or labelSelector when both are supplied.
cards.explanation: A Kustomize patch target combines its selection criteria. A resource must match both the supplied name and labelSelector for that patch to apply.
cards.misconception: Supplying a name and a labelSelector creates alternative ways to match the patch target.

cards.statement: Kustomize's namespace field leaves a namespaced resource's explicitly assigned namespace unchanged.
cards.explanation: The namespace transformer sets the namespace on namespaced resources, overriding namespace values already present in those resources.
cards.misconception: An existing namespace value takes precedence over the kustomization's namespace field.

cards.statement: By default, Kustomize automatically includes generated ConfigMaps when it applies namePrefix.
cards.explanation: The namePrefix transformation covers generated resources as well as resources loaded from manifests. A generated ConfigMap therefore receives the configured prefix.

cards.statement: The patches field accepts strategic merge patches and JSON 6902 patches in the same kustomization.
cards.explanation: Kustomize's patches list supports both patch formats. Entries may load a patch file or contain an inline patch.

cards.statement: When two patches set the same scalar field, Kustomize gives the first patch's value precedence.
cards.explanation: Kustomize applies patches in their listed order. A later patch that sets the same scalar field replaces the value left by an earlier patch.
cards.misconception: The first patch's value wins when another patch later changes the same field.

cards.statement: Kustomize automatically adds labels from the labels field to Deployment selectors by default.
cards.explanation: The labels field leaves selectors unchanged unless includeSelectors is true. Its default behavior adds the labels to resource metadata.
cards.misconception: The labels field changes selectors as part of its default behavior.

cards.statement: With includeTemplates true and includeSelectors false, Kustomize adds labels to a Deployment's Pod template.
cards.explanation: Setting includeTemplates to true includes Pod template metadata in the label transformation even when includeSelectors remains false.

cards.statement: Kubernetes keeps deprecated GA API versions available within the same major version.
cards.explanation: A GA API version can be deprecated while Kubernetes continues serving it within the same major version. Deprecation alone does not authorize its removal.

cards.statement: Kubernetes counts a beta API version's removal grace period from its original introduction.
cards.explanation: The beta removal window starts at deprecation. Kubernetes serves the version for at least nine months or three minor releases after that, whichever lasts longer.
cards.misconception: Beta API removal grace starts when the API version is first introduced.

cards.statement: Kubernetes gives alpha API versions the same advance removal notice as beta API versions.
cards.explanation: An upgrade can drop an alpha API endpoint even when the previous release gives no warning that the endpoint will disappear.
cards.misconception: Alpha API versions receive the same advance deprecation notice as beta versions.

cards.statement: The API server reads stored objects through the replacement API after removing their old endpoint.
cards.explanation: The replacement API still exposes objects saved using an older API version. Retiring the old endpoint changes how clients access those objects.

cards.statement: By default, `kubectl apply` returns an error when the API server warns about a deprecated API.
cards.explanation: kubectl apply prints server warnings and completes an otherwise successful request by default. Treating warnings as command errors requires opting into that behavior.
cards.misconception: A server warning about a deprecated API makes kubectl fail by default.

cards.statement: By default, `kubectl api-versions` discovers API versions from the connected server.
cards.explanation: kubectl api-versions uses server discovery to report what the connected cluster serves, so its result reflects the cluster's available APIs.

cards.statement: A fresh installation of the official kubectl binary includes the `kubectl convert` plugin.
cards.explanation: kubectl convert is distributed as a separate plugin binary. Install it separately before using it to migrate manifests between API versions.
cards.misconception: The kubectl binary bundles and installs the convert plugin.

source.title: Install and Set Up kubectl on Linux

cards.statement: Kubernetes v1.37 accepts new CronJobs submitted with `apiVersion: batch/v1beta1`.
cards.explanation: Use batch/v1 for current CronJob manifests. Kubernetes stopped serving the batch/v1beta1 CronJob endpoint in v1.25.
cards.misconception: Current Kubernetes clusters still accept the beta CronJob API version.

cards.statement: Since Kubernetes v1.33, the Kubernetes documentation recommends EndpointSlice over deprecated Endpoints.
cards.explanation: The deprecated Endpoints API has limitations such as truncated endpoint lists. Kubernetes directs API clients to EndpointSlice instead.
cards.volatilityNote: The Endpoints API is deprecated; its availability and migration guidance may change.

cards.statement: Since Kubernetes v1.37, the installed stable Metrics API also serves `metrics.k8s.io/v1beta1`.
cards.explanation: The stable metrics.k8s.io/v1 API coexists with v1beta1 during the transition. Existing beta clients can keep using the installed Metrics API.
cards.volatilityNote: Serving v1beta1 during the Metrics API transition is subject to future deprecation and removal.

cards.statement: The kubelet counts an exec probe as successful when the probe command exits with status zero.
cards.explanation: For an exec probe, the command's exit status determines the check result; zero signals success.

cards.statement: The kubelet marks an HTTP probe as failed when a same-host redirect leads to a successful response.
cards.explanation: The kubelet follows same-host redirects for HTTP probes and evaluates the final response.
cards.misconception: An HTTP redirect makes a probe fail despite a successful final response.

cards.statement: A TCP probe succeeds when the application accepts the connection and immediately closes it.
cards.explanation: A TCP probe checks whether it establishes a connection, even if the application immediately closes that connection.

cards.statement: A gRPC probe can invoke a custom RPC method named in the Pod manifest.
cards.explanation: Kubernetes gRPC probes call the standard gRPC Health Checking Protocol rather than a chosen application RPC method.
cards.misconception: A Kubernetes gRPC probe invokes a custom application RPC method selected in the Pod manifest.

source.title: Configure Liveness, Readiness and Startup Probes

cards.statement: The kubelet automatically waits for a startup probe to succeed before liveness or readiness probes run.
cards.explanation: A successful startup probe releases the gate that delays the container's liveness and readiness checks.

cards.statement: The kubelet waits for a readiness probe to succeed before beginning the container's liveness checks.
cards.explanation: Liveness checks run independently of readiness results; an unsuccessful readiness probe does not hold them back.
cards.misconception: Readiness success gates liveness checks.

source.title: Configure Liveness, Readiness and Startup Probes

cards.statement: The kubelet stops a container's readiness checks after the probe first reports a successful result.
cards.explanation: The kubelet keeps running readiness probes throughout a container's lifetime, checking for changes after initial success.
cards.misconception: Readiness probing finishes after its first successful check.

source.title: Configure Liveness, Readiness and Startup Probes

cards.statement: An aggressive liveness probe can increase load on surviving Pods by restarting overloaded containers.
cards.explanation: Probe-triggered restarts reduce serving capacity during overload, shifting work to remaining Pods and potentially causing further probe failures.

cards.statement: The API server accepts a readiness probe with its own `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` value.
cards.explanation: The API server rejects terminationGracePeriodSeconds in readiness probes because readiness failure leaves the container running.
cards.misconception: Readiness probes accept an individual termination grace period.

cards.statement: The API server rejects an ordinary init container that defines a `startupProbe`.
cards.explanation: Ordinary init containers do not support startupProbe, so the API server rejects that probe configuration.
